About

Data science that solves real problems

I'm a data scientist and a graduate of École Centrale Casablanca, where I studied data science and digitalization. Since June 2026 I have been a Data Scientist Confirmé at AXA Assurance Maroc, working on a machine-learning project to detect fraud in auto insurance.

Before AXA, I spent two and a half years building AI products end to end: a semantic search engine and manufacturing-time prediction models at Wineo Artificial Intelligence, then LLM agents, RAG chatbots and computer-vision applications at The Game Changer Company. Earlier internships in France and Morocco took me through deep learning for health data, object detection in operating rooms and industrial analytics.

What drives me is the same at every step: using data to unravel complex problems and make meaningful improvements in people's lives, with a strong belief in continuous learning and hard work.

Current roleData Scientist Confirmé, AXA Assurance Maroc FocusFraud detection · Machine learning · GenAI EducationÉcole Centrale Casablanca, M.Sc. Data Science (2023) Based inCasablanca, Morocco LanguagesFrench (DALF C1) · English (TOEIC 830)

Expertise

What I work on Fraud detection & machine learning

Machine learning applied to auto insurance fraud at AXA Assurance Maroc. Earlier: manufacturing-time prediction with one model per work centre, and classification with K-NN, CART and stacking ensembles.

Generative AI & LLM agents

Multi-step agents with LangGraph, RAG chatbots with LangChain and ChromaDB, semantic search, and local LLM stacks with Ollama and Open WebUI.

Computer vision

Object detection with YOLO, face and facial-attribute analysis, fine-tuned CNNs (VGG16, InceptionV3) and real-time people counting on the edge with NVIDIA Jetson Nano.

ML engineering & deployment

From notebook to production: FastAPI and Flask services, Docker, REST APIs, dashboards with Dash and Plotly, and deployments on OVH Cloud and on-premise servers.

items.title: Notes on AI
items.text:
Short reads on what's moving in artificial intelligence, through the eyes of a data scientist who works on fraud detection in insurance: what was announced, what it changes in practice, and what I would check before using it.

Opinions are my own and do not represent my employer.

items.title: AI near-misses as incidents: what the UK regulator's latest message means for fraud models
items.text:
On 19 October 2026, the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) sent a clear signal to banks and insurers. Its existing rules on reporting major incidents should also cover significant AI failures, and even near-misses. The same day, it published a review of good and poor practice for AI in financial services.

The FCA has no authority in Morocco. Still, its message is worth reading closely for anyone who runs machine-learning models in a regulated business. Most of it applies just as well to a classic fraud-detection model as to the latest large language model.
path: AI near-misses as incidents: what the UK regulator's latest message means for fraud models

items.title: What was said
items.text:
The message came in a speech by Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, at the Bloomberg UK Policy Series. The FCA has published the speech as drafted. Its main points:

  • Incidents: firms already have to report major incidents. In her words, that duty "must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses".
  • Agentic finance: the FCA plans to work with industry, other regulators and AI labs on a framework for AI agents acting in finance. It would cover agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.
  • Concentration risk: firms should understand their supplier dependencies, including reliance on a single model. They should stress-test their systems, plan for failure and keep fallback options.
  • Continuous assurance: an agentic system that is safe on day one can behave differently later, for example when the underlying model changes. Assurance has to be ongoing.
  • Disclaimers: AI providers are asked to state clearly the limits of the financial information their models produce.
  • Adoption: citing a joint FCA and Bank of England survey due the following week, she said 86% of firms now use AI.

At this stage this is a direction of travel, not a new rule. No consultation on AI incident reporting has been opened, and the FCA had not yet defined what counts as a "significant" failure or a near-miss.
path: AI near-misses as incidents: what the UK regulator's latest message means for fraud models

items.title: What the FCA's good-practice review says
items.text:
The publication, AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement, covers firms that develop, buy, deploy or use AI. It is organised around three themes: the Consumer Duty and vulnerable customers, governance and accountability, and operational resilience. It creates no new requirements and builds on existing rules. Among the practices it highlights:

  • keeping auditable records of prompts, outputs, model versions, filters and escalation decisions;
  • monitoring real-world outcomes and model drift in a forward-looking way, not only technical metrics;
  • requiring advance notice of significant model changes from vendors in contracts;
  • designing systems that can switch providers, with contingency and exit plans;
  • giving AI risks a named senior owner, accountable from the design stage.

The weaknesses it lists mirror these practices: dependence on a single provider without an exit plan, governance done after the fact, and monitoring that watches the model but not the outcomes for customers.
path: AI near-misses as incidents: what the UK regulator's latest message means for fraud models

items.title: Why this matters for fraud detection
items.text:
Fraud models are a textbook case of AI that affects customers. A model that scores claims decides, in practice, which files get a fast payout and which get an investigation. Read with that in mind, the FCA's points translate quite directly. What follows is my own analysis.

What a near-miss could look like. Imagine a model update that suddenly doubles the number of legitimate claims flagged as suspicious. Investigators catch it within a week and roll back. No customer was harmed for long, but many waited longer than they should have. Under the approach the FCA describes, that is exactly the kind of event a firm may one day need to detect, document and possibly report.

What I would put in place, whatever the jurisdiction:

  1. Version everything. Training data snapshot, features, model, thresholds and the code that applies them. You cannot explain an incident you cannot reproduce.
  2. Monitor outcomes, not just AUC. Track alert rates, investigation outcomes, false positives and processing delays, by segment. Drift in the population often shows up there before it shows up in model metrics.
  3. Define incident thresholds in advance. Decide now which change in alert volume or precision triggers an investigation, a rollback or an escalation.
  4. Keep a fallback. A previous model version or a rules-based baseline you can switch to while you investigate.
  5. Name an owner. A model in production needs an accountable person outside the data science team, who understands what it does and signs off on changes.

None of this is new to good MLOps practice. What is changing is that regulators are starting to expect it, and to call the failures by their name.
path: AI near-misses as incidents: what the UK regulator's latest message means for fraud models

items.title: Meta opens the weights of an 816B agentic model: what it changes for regulated data teams
items.text:
On 15 October 2026, Meta released Muse Spark Open, a large open-weight model trained for agentic work: reading large codebases, calling tools, checking results and recovering when a step fails. The weights are on Hugging Face, so anyone can download and run the model on their own infrastructure.

For teams in banking and insurance, "open weights" sounds like the answer to a recurring problem: how to use a frontier-class model without sending customer data to an external API. The reality is more nuanced. Here is what was actually released, what it takes to run it, and what I would check before using it on sensitive data.
path: Meta opens the weights of an 816B agentic model: what it changes for regulated data teams

items.title: What Meta released
items.text:
According to Meta's announcement and the Hugging Face release notes:

  • Architecture: a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with about 816 billion parameters in total, of which only about 42 billion are active for each token. It has 62 layers with 256 experts each, and 8 experts are used per token.
  • Context: up to 1 million tokens.
  • Modalities: it reads text, images, audio and video, and answers in text.
  • Purpose: Meta presents it as trained for long-horizon agentic tasks such as coding agents and customer-service agents.
  • Checkpoints: a full-precision BF16 version (about 1.6 TB) and an NVFP4 version quantized by Meta (about 530 GB, with only the experts quantized).

A mixture-of-experts model works like a large team of specialists: for each token, a router picks a handful of experts instead of running the whole network. That is why "816B" and "42B" can both be true. The compute per token is close to that of a 42B model, but all 816B parameters still have to sit in memory.
path: Meta opens the weights of an 816B agentic model: what it changes for regulated data teams

items.title: Open weights, but not small
items.text:
That memory footprint is the first reality check. Meta says the NVFP4 checkpoint runs on four Blackwell Ultra GPUs or eight H200s, and on two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 512 GB of memory each. Community quantizations go further: Hugging Face reports a 2-bit build using about 304 GB on a 512 GB Mac.

So, yes, the model can run on premises, which keeps data inside your walls. But it needs hardware that few data teams have under their desks. The alternative Meta offers is hosted access through Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq (limited preview), Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI, and through the model catalogs of Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry.

That is convenient, but it brings back the question open weights were supposed to remove: your data is processed by a third party again.
path: Meta opens the weights of an 816B agentic model: what it changes for regulated data teams

items.title: Read the licence before the benchmarks
items.text:
The weights are open, but the model is not "free of conditions". The Muse Model License includes, among other terms:

  • an obligation to display "Built with Muse Spark Open" in any product or service that uses it;
  • for companies that offer AI models to third parties as an API service and earn more than US$20 million in gross revenue over 12 months, an obligation to notify Meta and sign a separate agreement first (internal use and using the model inside your own product are excluded);
  • a usage policy that forbids the unlicensed practice of financial, legal or medical professions, and facilitating discrimination in employment, credit, housing or access to essential goods and services.

That last point matters for insurance and lending. An LLM that helps triage claims or summarise customer files sits close to decisions about people. Whether a given use case is compatible with these terms is a question for your legal team, not for a benchmark table.
path: Meta opens the weights of an 816B agentic model: what it changes for regulated data teams

items.title: Where it stands
items.text: In Meta's own comparison table, Muse Spark Open scores 39 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. That is ahead of Mistral Large 4 (38), but behind Qwen3.8 (40), Kimi K3 (44) and GLM 5.3 (45). Meta presents it as the most capable open-weight model released by a US company so far. These are vendor-reported figures. As always, the only benchmark that counts is your own task, on your own data.
path: Meta opens the weights of an 816B agentic model: what it changes for regulated data teams

items.title: My take as a data scientist in insurance
items.text:
Three practical thoughts, which are my own opinion:

  1. Open weights are a sovereignty option, not a free lunch. Running an 816B model on premises is a real infrastructure project. For many tasks, such as extracting fields from claim documents, classifying e-mails or drafting summaries, a much smaller open model, fine-tuned and evaluated properly, will be cheaper, faster and easier to govern.
  2. Hosted "open" is still outsourcing. If you call the model through a cloud provider, apply the same due diligence as for any external API: where the data goes, how long it is kept, and whether personal data rules (such as Morocco's Law 09-08) allow the transfer.
  3. Agents need guardrails before autonomy. A model trained to call tools and act over long tasks is powerful. In a regulated process, every action it takes should be logged and reversible, and a human should stay accountable for the decision.

In fraud detection, the core models remain classic machine learning on structured data. Large language models are most useful around them: reading unstructured documents, explaining alerts to investigators, and speeding up reviews. Muse Spark Open widens the menu of options for that work. It does not remove the need to measure, document and keep a human in the loop.
